planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Hummel's Sunset needs strong light to develop its best coloring.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, since this cultivar needs strong light to develop its signature coloring. Rounded, glossy green leaves are broadly edged in creamy yellow that blushes pink to red along the margins in bright light or cool weather, a striking variegated sport of the common jade plant. Like other jade cultivars it is slow-growing and long-lived, eventually forming a thick, woody, tree-like trunk that suits container bonsai styling. Water only once the soil has dried out fully, and propagate from stem or leaf cuttings allowed to callus for a day before rooting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; low light causes the variegation of Tricolor to fade toward solid green.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, since low light causes the variegation to fade toward solid green. Fleshy, oval leaves are striped in cream, white, and green, often flushed with pink to red along the margins when stressed by bright sun or cool nights, giving the plant its three-tone common name. It shares the easy care and drought tolerance of the standard jade plant, slowly developing thick, woody stems as it matures into a small, tree-like specimen suited to bonsai training. Because variegated leaf tissue lacks chlorophyll, growth is slower than the all-green species, and any reverted all-green shoots should be pruned out to keep the variegation strong.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings after the cut end has callused for a couple of days, then insert into gritty succulent mix and keep barely moist until roots take hold.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot or hanging basket with fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in bright light to partial sun, letting the mix dry out completely between waterings. Thick, triangular, blue-green leaves edged in red are stacked in tightly overlapping opposite pairs along woody, upright-then-trailing stems, creating a distinctive segmented, accordion-like pattern that gives the plant its common name. Closely related to the popular String of Buttons (Crassula perforata) but with more compact, rounded leaf pairs and a sturdier, shrubbier habit, it clusters into a dense mound over time and sends up small clusters of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers in late winter. Propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus for a couple of days before inserting into dry succulent mix.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to gentle morning sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; strong midday sun can scorch its soft, hairy leaves.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, indirect light to gentle morning sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, since strong midday sun can scorch its soft, hairy leaves. This compact hybrid between Crassula falcata and Crassula mesembryanthemoides forms tight, symmetrical rosettes of thick, gray-green, felted leaves edged with fine silvery hairs, a texture distinct from the smooth-leaved crassulas more commonly grown. Dense, rounded clusters of small coral-pink to red flowers rise on short stalks above the foliage in summer, adding seasonal color to its year-round rosette form. It stays low and slow-growing, making it well suited to a shallow dish or mixed succulent bowl, and is propagated from offsets or leaf cuttings rooted in dry succulent mix.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or as a xeriscape groundcover in bright light to partial sun in lean, fast-draining, gritty soil; water only once the mix has dried out completely.

directions: Grow in a shallow pot or as a groundcover in a xeriscape succulent bed in bright light to partial sun in lean, fast-draining, gritty soil, watering only when the mix has dried out completely. Small, tightly packed, gray-green rosettes edged in fine reddish hairs spread by offsets to form a dense, low mat, a mounding growth habit that gives the species both its common and scientific names. In late winter to early spring, mature clumps send up small clusters of white, star-shaped flowers held just above the foliage on short stems. Native to rocky outcrops in South Africa's Western Cape, it is a slow, low-maintenance succulent well suited to rock garden crevices, trough plantings, or the front edge of a mixed succulent container.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or hanging basket in bright, indirect light to gentle morning sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, out of harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or hanging basket in bright, indirect light to gentle morning sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, keeping it out of harsh afternoon sun that can scorch the leaves. Glossy, rounded, scalloped-edged leaves form a low rosette from which long, wiry runners trail outward, each tipped with a small plantlet that roots readily wherever it touches soil, a distinctive means of vegetative spread that gives the species its common name. Clusters of small, tubular, coral to salmon flowers may appear on mature plants above the foliage. Because of its trailing, self-propagating runners, it looks its best in a hanging basket or raised container where the plantlet-tipped stems can cascade freely, and division of rooted plantlets is the easiest way to start new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings. Large, upright, gray-green, paddle-shaped leaves marked with irregular maroon blotches form a substantial rosette on a stout stem, distinctly larger and bolder than most other kalanchoe succulents grown as houseplants. Tiny plantlets form along the leaf margins, especially on damaged or aging leaves, and drop off readily to root nearby, so keep an eye on wandering seedlings in a shared container. Mature plants send up a tall flowering stalk of pendant, greenish-pink, bell-shaped flowers, after which the main rosette typically declines, though offsets and plantlets carry the plant on.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Sugar Pilea (Speckled Variegated Chinese Money Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-draining, peat-based potting mix, keeping the variegated leaves out of direct sun, which scorches the pale patches.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light near an east- or north-facing window in a well-draining, peat-based houseplant potting mix, keeping variegated leaves out of direct sun, which scorches the pale sugar-white patches. Sugar is a stable variegated sport of the standard Chinese money plant, its round, peltate leaves speckled and marbled with irregular splashes of white to cream across the glossy green surface, giving each leaf a frosted, sugar-dusted look. Because the white tissue lacks chlorophyll, growth is slower and less vigorous than the all-green species, and pups that emerge fully green or with little variegation should be removed to keep the parent plant's energy focused on well-patterned growth. Propagate by potting up rooted offsets that form at the base of the main stem, and rotate the pot regularly for even, symmetrical growth.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Pilea peperomioides cultivation
American Nurseryman — Pilea peperomioides cultural notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pilea species for indoor culture

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a well-draining, peat-based potting mix, avoiding direct sun that can scorch the lighter patches of foliage.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light near an east- or north-facing window in a well-draining, peat-based houseplant potting mix, avoiding direct sun that can scorch the lighter patches of foliage. Mojito is a splash-variegated sport of the standard Chinese money plant, its round, peltate leaves marked with irregular yellow-green to chartreuse blotches scattered unevenly across a darker green background, no two leaves patterned quite alike. Variegation intensity shifts with light levels and can fade toward solid green on older leaves or on offsets grown in lower light, so bright, consistent light helps keep the pattern strong. Propagate by separating and potting up the plantlets, or pups, that form at the base of the main stem and along the soil surface, discarding any that emerge without variegation if a strongly patterned clump is the goal.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Pilea peperomioides cultivation
